entry.evidence: a comprehensive study of its mechanism and source features and their spectral parameters is important for future ground motion modulation studies

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text, with PDF for figures)

steps.action: Summarized earlier focal-mechanism studies of the northern Red Sea and Gulf of Aqaba as the regional background: normal faulting with NW–SE planes versus strike-slip with NNE–SSW planes.
steps.quote: shear stress results in normal movement, with a minor strike-slip component and nodal planes oriented NW–SE

steps.action: Compiled historical and instrumental catalogues (Maamoun to ENSN) into a seismicity map of the northern Red Sea, Gulf of Suez and Gulf of Aqaba.
steps.quote: A seismicity map created for the study area includes historical and instrumental seismic events

steps.action: Took the live 16 June 2020 ML 5.4 mainshock and its significant aftershocks (to 23 August 2020) as recorded by ENSN broadband stations, plus a few GEOFON stations added for azimuthal coverage.
steps.quote: The selected earthquakes were monitored by the broadband three-component seismic stations of the ENSN.

steps.action: Relocated the 30 events with HYPOINVERSE-ATLAS (mainshock at 4 km depth, aftershocks 8.8–28.6 km; average RMS 0.17 s, ERH 1.47 km, ERZ 0.98 km).
steps.quote: The data set was relocated using the HYPOINVERSE-ATLAS package

steps.action: Prepared the mainshock waveforms: removed mean and trend, resampled, tapered, removed the instrument response, rotated and filtered them, and kept only traces with good signal-to-noise ratio.
steps.quote: Only earthquakes with a good signal-to-noise ratio were used for the analysis

steps.action: Inverted the full-waveform moment tensor of the mainshock against wavenumber-integration Green's functions (Hosny et al. 2009 velocity model, 0.02–0.06 Hz) by least squares, choosing depth and mechanism by fit goodness; the result was strike-slip with a minor normal component, Mw 5.26, depth 3 km (Fig. 5A, p. 7).
steps.quote: full inversion of the moment tensor was applied to selected traces

steps.action: Extracted S-wave windows (2.56 s, starting 0.5 s before the picked S arrival) from three-component records, computed FFT spectra, smoothed them with a 5 Hz Hanning window and averaged them over stations.
steps.quote: the waveforms were selected from time windows with a of length 2.56 s starting 0.5 s before the manually picked S-phase arrivals

steps.action: Tested the reference-site premise of the generalized spectral inversion by running the inversion three times with KAT, HRG or BST as reference site (using each station's H/V curve), then chose KAT as the most reasonable.
steps.quote: the spectral inversion was carried out three times using one of the three stations as an alternative reference site

steps.action: Separated source spectra from attenuation and site effects (Andrews 1986; Iwata and Irikura 1988), fitted Brune's omega-square model and Andrews' automated corner frequency, and derived Mo, Mw, source radius and stress drop for the 30 events (Mw 2.4–5.0, fc 2.2–8.2 Hz, r 171–633 m, Δσ 0.02–13 MPa; Table 3).
steps.quote: The corner frequency was calculated for each source spectra using Andrews’s (6) automated method.

steps.action: Stated the two nodal planes of the best double couple (NNE–SSW and ESE–WNW) as the candidate fault planes.
steps.quote: with NNE–SSW and ESE–WNW trending fault planes

steps.action: Checked the waveform-inversion source depth against the depth from arrival-time relocation and reported them consistent (Fig. 5B, p. 7).
steps.quote: The relocated parameters especially the source depth of the mainshock are consistent with the optimum fitting source depth obtained in this study

steps.action: Compared the aftershock distribution with the two nodal planes to pick the fault plane; Results name NNE–SSW, while the abstract names ESE–WNW (Fig. 5C, p. 7).
steps.quote: [...] aftershocks selected in this study revealed that the plane oriented NNE–SSW toward the Gulf of Suez is the fault plane

steps.action: Reported that the aftershocks lie deeper than the mainshock and to its northwest, so they do not coincide with it in map view or in depth.
steps.quote: the aftershocks sequences distribution did not coincide with the 16 Jun, 2020 main earthquake, neither in map view nor with respect to depth

steps.action: Regressed the estimated Mw and log Mo on the ENSN local magnitudes and found a linear relation (Mw = 0.8ML + 0.67, R² = 0.83; Fig. 9, p. 11).
steps.quote: The assigned local magnitude catalog derived from the ENSN shows a linear relationship with the determined moment magnitude Mw

steps.action: Plotted the source parameters against seismic moment and depth: fc decreases and r and Δσ increase with Mo, and a possible depth dependence appears (Figs. 10–11, pp. 11–12).
steps.quote: the stress drop values increase with the increasing seismic moment of the current earthquakes’ sequences

steps.action: Compared the stress axes of the fault-plane solution with the regional extension of the Red Sea and found them consistent.
steps.quote: which is consistent with the general tension movement along [...]

steps.action: Proposed two untested explanations for the offset aftershock cluster: activation of a secondary fault, or stress triggering by the mainshock (citing Donner et al. 2013).
steps.quote: may indicated a secondary fault plane activation, or suggested that the seismicity in the north western side were activated

steps.action: Compared the best double-couple mechanism with published focal mechanisms of the region and found it consistent (Fig. 5D, p. 7).
steps.quote: was consistent with previous findings

steps.action: Restated the depth comparison, waveform depth 3 km against relocation depth 4 km.
steps.quote: The focal depth of the June 16, 2020 earthquake was very shallow (3 km) compared to the 4 km obtained by the relocation analysis.

steps.action: Compared the stress drops with Kanamori's (1994) 0.1–100 MPa range for small-to-moderate interplate earthquakes and reported good agreement.
steps.quote: The calculated stress drop values are in good agreement with the stress drop range of small-to-moderate interplate earthquakes

steps.action: Kept the spectral source parameters and the strike-slip mechanism as the characterization of the sequence, for use in hazard assessment.
steps.quote: Based on the shear-wave spectral inversion and Brune’s modulation, the spectral parameters using the isolated S-wave displacement spectra were determined.

tree.answer: The 16 June 2020 ML 5.4 northern Red Sea earthquake and its aftershocks
No; mechanism and source parameters are inferred from waveforms and spectra
Characterize the source mechanism and spectral source parameters for hazard studies
Two nodal planes as candidate fault planes; secondary fault activation versus stress triggering for the aftershocks
Only for the nodal planes, through the aftershock alignment; the verdict is stated inconsistently
Found: a live event recorded by the national network
Limited checks: reference station varied, relocation depth against waveform depth, Mw against ML
Source parameters and mechanism kept as estimates; aftershock explanation left open

end.claim: The 16 June 2020 mainshock was strike-slip with a minor normal component, and the sequence's source parameters range over Mo 8.293E+18 to 7.541E+22 dyn·cm, Mw 2.4–5.0, fc 2.2–8.2 Hz, r 171–633 m and Δσ 0.02–13 MPa, with stress drop increasing with event size.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the full-waveform moment tensor inversion and the reference-site spectral inversion with Brune fitting, neither the mechanism nor any source parameter would exist.

gates.evidence: The data are routine network recordings of a found event; no hypothesis directed their acquisition. The estimates face only weak checks that could have failed: the relocation depth (4 km) against the waveform depth (3 km), Mw against the ENSN ML, and published mechanisms and the stress-drop range. The 0.02–0.06 Hz band was taken from literature recommendations, but nothing is described as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Fast Fourier transform with Hanning-window smoothing of spectra
Eshelby (1957) elastic inclusion solution used for the stress drop of a circular fault

limits:
No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

Internal inconsistencies:
- Fault plane: the Results name the NNE–SSW plane as the fault plane (§5.1 ¶1), but the abstract says the aftershock clustering supports the ESE–WNW plane (§0 ¶1). Inference: a cluster to the northwest is more naturally read as support for the ESE–WNW plane. The fault-plane sub-claim therefore has no stable status.
- Mainshock size: moment tensor Mw is 5.26 (Fig. 5A, p. 7), spectral Mw is 5.0 (Table 3), and ML is given as 5.4 in the text but 5.5 in Table 1.
- Stress axes: the T-axis and P-axis are both said to trend ENE–WSW (§6 ¶1); inference: a typographical error.
- Stress-drop range: the lowest value (0.02 MPa) falls below the cited Kanamori range of 0.1–100 MPa, yet the paper reports good agreement (§6 ¶2).
- Depth dependence: the Results say the parameters 'may be' depth dependent (§5.2 ¶2), but the conclusion states it as a finding (§6 ¶2).

Uncertainty and checks:
- No uncertainties are given for the individual source parameters; only spectral standard deviations (Fig. 7B) and waveform fit (95%, Fig. 6) are shown. The 'accurate and robust' statement rests on fit quality, not on a variation test.
- The reference-site test does not report how the alternative reference stations change the results.

Sub-claims:
- Scaling relations with Mo and the Mw–ML regression: regularity_in_range, sparse and driven by the single mainshock point.
- Secondary fault versus stress triggering for the aftershocks: hypothesis only, untested.
- Fault-plane choice: none (inconsistent).

Composition: none_fits, because the walk is a single-event estimation with no rival test, a found event that nature does not repeat, and no new capability. The aftershock scaling has a natures_repetition flavour, but the regularity is not the headline.

Data are not public (available from NRIAG on request).
